title: At-Takwir: the buried girl
hook: when the baby girl buried alive is asked for what sin she was killed (81:8–9)

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Takwir, the sun wound up like a turban and put away. Your line was everything ends but him. Did something feel a little lighter? Day two hundred twelve.

Among the twelve whens of At-Takwir, the sun wrapped, the stars falling, the seas on fire, there is one that isn't about the sky at all. It's about a single child. Of everything the surah could have chosen to show on the last day, the biggest events in the universe, it stops for one small girl whom nobody in her own world stopped for. Today's lesson is a hard one, and it's told gently. It's about who gets to speak on that day, and who has to answer. Today: the buried girl.
screen: `THE SUN, THE STARS, THE SEAS.` → `AND ONE SMALL GIRL.` → `THE BURIED GIRL.`

segments.voice: Verses eight and nine, in Pickthall's words: "And when the girl-child that was buried alive is asked For what sin she was slain." Commentators say that in pre-Islamic Arabia some people killed newborn daughters. The Qur'an itself names two reasons: fear of poverty, and fear of shame. The Qur'an describes the reaction elsewhere: when one of them is told a daughter has been born, his face darkens, and he hides from people, wondering whether to keep her in humiliation or bury her in the dust. The Qur'an forbade it outright: do not kill your children for fear of poverty. Now look closely at how verse nine is built. The question isn't put to the father. It's put to her. For what sin was she killed? Commentators notice this. The one who had no voice in her short life is the one addressed on that day, in front of everyone, and her answer will be the testimony. And the question itself contains its answer: no sin. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ went further than forbidding. A hadith in Muslim's collection says that whoever raises two daughters until they grow up will come on the Day of Resurrection with him, and he held his fingers together to show how close. He had daughters himself, and was known for standing up to greet Fatima when she came into the room. So the surah names the harm, gives the girl the question, and the Prophet's practice turns the shame upside down: raising a daughter becomes a way to be close to him.
screen: `AL-MAW'UDAH — THE BURIED GIRL.` · `FEAR OF POVERTY, FEAR OF SHAME.` · `THE QUESTION IS PUT TO HER.` · `RAISING DAUGHTERS, CLOSE TO HIM.` · then, large: `SHE WILL BE ASKED.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, bring to mind a girl or woman in your life. A daughter, a sister, a niece, a mother, a student, a friend. Picture her face. Think of one thing about her that deserves to be honored out loud: her courage, her humor, her work. Then decide how you'll tell her, today. If there's no one close, hold in mind girls anywhere whose lives aren't valued. The bell holds the time.
At-Takwir. The wrapping up, Surah eighty-one, where the buried girl is asked for what sin she was killed. Today's word.
Your line: she will be asked. Honor one girl or woman today, in words she can hear, for something real. Day two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Muslims read these verses as the Qur'an's condemnation of female infanticide; the hadith on raising daughters is quoted at the birth of a girl, and the 'aqiqah, a sacrifice and a shared meal of thanks, is held for daughters as well as sons.

myth: every tribe in pre-Islamic Arabia buried infant daughters
the sources describe some people doing it, not everyone; the Qur'an forbade it outright.
in 81:9 the question is put to the girl, not to her killer
commentators note the one with no voice is the one addressed.
the Prophet Muhammad had only sons
he had daughters, and was known for rising to greet his daughter Fatima.

fork.setup: on the last day, a question is asked about the girl who was buried alive. who is it put to?
fork.reveal: she is asked, for what sin she was slain (81:8–9). the one silenced in life is given the question, and the answer is: none.

original.note: Arabic: the girl buried alive, from w-'-d, to bury a newborn (Qur'an 81:8).

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient cruelty the Qur'an mentions.
what it means: the Qur'an forbids it, and on the last day gives the murdered girl herself the question.

what a scholar hears: commentators read su'ilat, she is asked, as addressing the victim to shame the killer; 16:58–59 describes the darkened face at a daughter's birth; 6:151 and 17:31 forbid killing children for fear of poverty.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): pre-Islamic infanticide now framed as what commentators say, with the reasons the Qur'an itself names (poverty, shame); cut the unsourced 'captured in a raid' and 'sons as wealth' claims and the 'some tribes, not all' head; howItsDone drops 'many families' and 'often'.
Please confirm the exact Pickthall wording of 81:8–9.
Muslim 2631 and Abu Dawud 5217 / Tirmidhi 3872 cited from memory; confirm.

Four daughters (Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatima) is the Sunni account; some Shia scholars hold Fatima was his only biological daughter. The script says only 'he had daughters' so both views are respected.
'Some tribes, not all' on pre-Islamic infanticide: confirm the historical framing.
'aqiqah for daughters in howItsDone: practice varies (commonly one sheep for a girl, two for a boy in Sunni fiqh); the script doesn't claim equality of the sacrifice.
